paragraphs.body:
Preparing commercial gutters for winter means clearing leaves and debris, checking downspouts for clogs, inspecting gutters and hangers for damage, and making sure water drains away from the building. These steps help reduce the risk of ice dams, overflow, and water damage during New England winters. Scheduling commercial gutter cleaning in late fall, after most leaves have dropped, gives your property the best start to the season.

For property managers overseeing apartment buildings, condominiums, and office properties, gutters are easy to overlook until something goes wrong. At Air Tech Solutions, we've served commercial properties across New England since 2010, and this checklist covers what to address before freezing weather arrives.

Flat-roof commercial buildings often rely on roof drains and scuppers rather than traditional gutters. These drains can also clog with leaves and debris. Include them in your fall inspection so water can drain freely during winter thaws.
Photos and notes from fall inspections help track gutter condition over time. Records support budgeting for repairs and help maintenance teams spot recurring problem areas.
Winter storms can bring down branches and debris. Plan a spring inspection to check for damage and clear any new buildup.

Gutters move water away from the roof, walls, and foundation. When they're clogged, water can overflow, freeze, and create problems. In winter, clogged gutters can contribute to ice buildup along roof edges, which may lead to leaks.

Preventative maintenance helps protect the property and reduce emergency calls.

Clear Leaves and Debris

Remove leaves, twigs, and debris from gutters and downspouts. Late fall cleaning, after most leaves have fallen, is usually most effective.

Check Downspouts

Make sure downspouts are clear and water flows freely. Clogged downspouts can send water back into gutters.

Inspect Gutters and Hangers

Look for sagging sections, loose hangers, and separated joints. Damaged gutters may not drain properly.

Confirm Drainage Away From the Building

Check that downspouts direct water away from foundations, walkways, and entrances. Water pooling near walkways can freeze and create slip hazards.

Look for Signs of Past Overflow

Staining on siding, worn landscaping, or erosion below gutters can point to past overflow problems.

• Water spilling over gutters during rain
  • Visible plants or debris in gutters
  • Sagging or separated gutter sections
  • Staining on exterior walls
  • Ice buildup along roof edges in past winters

title.rendered: Sealing and Caulking Before a New England Winter

blog_post.title: Sealing and Caulking Before a New England Winter
blog_post.excerpt: Sealing and caulking before winter means finding the gaps, cracked joints, and worn seals on a building's exterior and closing them while the weather still…

main_image.alt: Worker applying caulk around a window frame

thumbnail_image.alt: Worker applying caulk around a window frame

paragraphs.body:
Sealing and caulking before winter means finding the gaps, cracked joints, and worn seals on a building's exterior and closing them while the weather still allows. Water that gets into those openings freezes, expands, and widens them. A walk-through in early fall gives property managers time to plan the work before freeze-thaw cycles and winter storms arrive.

This guide covers where to look, what to look for, and how to decide what needs a professional. It is written for property managers, facility managers, and condominium associations responsible for larger buildings.

paragraphs.header: Why Does Sealing Matter Before Winter in New England?
paragraphs.body:
New England weather moves back and forth across the freezing point many times each season. Water slips into a small gap on a mild afternoon. It freezes overnight and expands. By morning, the gap is a little wider.

That cycle is called freeze-thaw. Repeated over a winter, it can turn a hairline crack into a path for moisture into walls, insulation, and interior finishes. Sealant is the flexible material that fills joints and gaps to keep water and air out. Caulk is one common type.

Sealing is routine preventive maintenance. It does not make a building immune to moisture problems, but it removes some of the easiest ways for water to get in.

paragraphs.header: Where Should Property Managers Look for Exterior Gaps and Joints?
paragraphs.body:
Start with the places where two materials meet. Different materials expand and contract at different rates, so those seams take the most stress.

Windows and doors

Check the perimeter where frames meet the wall. Look for sealant that has pulled away, split, or turned brittle. Entrance doors and storefront frames get heavy use, so they deserve a close look.

Building joints and penetrations

Look at control joints in masonry and siding, and at the points where pipes, vents, conduit, and light fixtures pass through the wall. Each opening needs an intact seal around it.

Balconies, railings, and transitions

On apartment and condominium buildings, check where balcony slabs meet the wall and where railing posts meet the surface. These spots collect water and often show wear first.

Rooflines and trim

Inspect fascia, soffits, and the areas around gutters and downspouts. Gutters that overflow can push water against joints that were never meant to stay wet. Our post on what property managers should know before scheduling a commercial gutter cleaning project covers how clear gutters and sound seals work together.

paragraphs.header: What Does Worn Sealant Look Like?
paragraphs.body:
You do not need a trained eye to spot most problems. Walk the perimeter on a dry day and look for these signs:

  • Cracks, splits, or gaps in the bead of sealant
  • Sealant that has shrunk, pulled away from an edge, or peeled off
  • Hard, chalky, or crumbly material in place of a flexible bead
  • Staining or streaking below a joint
  • Daylight visible around a frame, or drafts felt near it
  • Interior water marks near windows, doors, or exterior walls

A single sign does not always mean a failure. Several signs in one area usually justify a closer look.

Not every joint needs attention at once. A simple ranking helps teams plan the work and the budget.

Start with the joints most exposed to wind-driven rain and snow, which are often on the north and west faces of a building. Then address areas where you have already received tenant or resident reports of leaks or drafts. Finally, look at upper floors and hard-to-reach spots, which are easy to overlook from the ground.

Multi-story buildings often need special access to reach those upper joints safely. We use boom lifts and rope access for this kind of work, which lets crews reach difficult areas without scaffolding the whole building.

paragraphs.header: How Do Cleaning and Sealing Work Together?
paragraphs.body:
Sealant bonds best to a clean, dry surface. Dirt, algae, and mildew can keep a new bead from holding well. Cleaning the area first, often with gentle soft washing, helps the work last.

Moisture-loving growth on exterior walls is common in this region. If you see it, our post on why New England buildings struggle with algae and mildew explains what causes it and how to address it.

For a broader fall checklist, see what a commercial property exterior should look like going into winter.

paragraphs.header: When Should You Call a Professional?
paragraphs.body:
Small touch-ups at a ground-floor door may be something your maintenance team handles. Call a professional when:

  • Joints are on upper floors or other areas that require lifts or rope access
  • Old sealant needs to be removed before new material goes in
  • The same joint has failed more than once
  • You are sealing around windows, penetrations, or building envelope transitions
  • The work covers a large property or many buildings

A professional crew also matches the sealant to the joint. Different materials and movement levels call for different products, and the wrong choice can fail early.

paragraphs.header: How Does Timing Work for Fall Sealing?
paragraphs.body:
Sealants need suitable temperatures and dry conditions to cure properly. Product requirements vary, so check the manufacturer's guidance for the material being used. In New England, that generally makes early to mid fall the more practical window, before nights turn consistently cold.

Scheduling early also leaves room for weather delays. Occupied buildings add another layer, so it helps to plan access and notices to residents in advance. Our post on what to coordinate before a dryer vent or exhaust cleaning project in an occupied building offers a useful framework that applies to exterior work as well.

How often should commercial building sealant be inspected?

Many property teams inspect exterior joints at least once a year, with fall being a practical time. After severe storms, a quick look at exposed areas is also worthwhile.

How long does exterior sealant last?

It depends on the product, the joint, and sun and weather exposure. Sealant is a wear item, and it eventually needs replacing. A professional assessment can tell you where yours stands.

Can sealing stop all water and air leaks?

No. Sealing closes common entry points, but leaks can also come from roofing, flashing, drainage, and other building components. A walk-through helps identify the likely source.

Can sealing be done on an occupied property?

Yes, in most cases. Good planning around access, notices, and work areas keeps disruption to tenants and residents low.

How do I request a quote for exterior sealing work?

Share the property type, number of buildings and stories, and the areas of concern, along with any photos you have. That gives us what we need to scope the work.

blog_post.title: Which Commercial Buildings Need HVAC Cleaning Most?
blog_post.excerpt: Multi-family properties, healthcare facilities, and hotels tend to need commercial HVAC cleaning most often.

main_image.alt: Rooftop HVAC units and ductwork on a commercial building

thumbnail_image.alt: Rooftop HVAC units and ductwork on a commercial building

paragraphs.body:
Multi-family properties, healthcare facilities, and hotels tend to need commercial HVAC cleaning most often. These buildings have high occupancy, long system run times, and constant foot traffic, so their systems collect dust, debris, and moisture faster than those in a lightly used building.

If you manage one of these properties, the right schedule depends on how your building is used, not on a single calendar rule. This post walks through the property types that tend to need attention more often, why, and how to spot the signs that your system is ready for a professional look.

HVAC stands for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning. Commercial HVAC cleaning removes built-up dust, debris, and residue from parts of the system that move and condition air, such as ductwork, vents, and related components.

Think of it like a building's lungs. When airflow is clear, the system moves air the way it was designed to. When buildup collects, the system works harder and airflow can suffer. Cleaning is one part of a larger preventative maintenance plan, and it works alongside filter changes and routine inspections.

paragraphs.header: What Businesses Need Commercial HVAC Cleaning the Most?
paragraphs.body:
Three things drive how quickly a system gets dirty: how many people use the building, how many hours the system runs, and how much moisture and outside debris enters the space. Buildings that rank high on all three tend to need cleaning more often.

The sections below cover the property types we see this in most.

Why Do Multi-Family Properties Need More Frequent Cleaning?

Apartment buildings, condominiums, and townhome communities have people home at all hours. Systems run around the clock in many cases, and every unit adds cooking, bathing, laundry, and daily living to the air handling load.

Hotels combine heavy occupancy, frequent turnover, and guests who notice comfort right away. A room that smells stale or runs too warm shows up in a review quickly.

A busy multi-tenant office with many occupants has different needs than a quiet suite. blog_post.excerpt: Most multi-family buildings should have their dryer vents professionally cleaned at least once a year, and some need it every six months or more often.

main_image.alt: Exterior dryer vent hood clogged with lint

thumbnail_image.alt: Exterior dryer vent hood clogged with lint

paragraphs.body:
Most multi-family buildings should have their dryer vents professionally cleaned at least once a year, and some need it every six months or more often. The right schedule depends on building size, vent length, the number of units on each system, and how heavily residents use their dryers.

A single number rarely fits every property. A three-story garden-style complex with short, straight vents has different needs than a six-story building with long runs that travel through walls and up to the roof. This guide walks through the factors that set a schedule, so you can build one that fits your property.

paragraphs.header: Why does one schedule not fit every apartment building?
paragraphs.body:
Dryer vents carry hot, moist air and lint out of the building. Lint that the dryer's own filter misses settles inside the duct. Over time, that buildup restricts airflow.

How quickly that happens varies from building to building. Two properties with the same unit count can collect lint at very different rates. That is why a schedule works best when it starts with the building itself, not a calendar default.

paragraphs.header: What factors set the cleaning schedule?
paragraphs.body:
Five factors do most of the work. Look at each one for your property.

How long is the vent run?

Longer vents hold more lint and move air less easily. Every bend adds resistance, and long runs with several turns tend to build up faster than short, straight ones. Vents that run through multiple floors or to a distant roof termination often need more frequent attention.

How many units share a system?

Some buildings give each unit its own vent. Others use shared vertical risers that serve several units. Shared systems collect lint from many dryers at once, so a problem in one unit can affect airflow for others.

How heavily do residents use their dryers?

Large households, family-oriented communities, and buildings with in-unit washers and dryers on every floor generate more lint than a small building of single occupants. Heavy use means faster buildup. If you manage a mix of unit types, plan around your busiest areas.

What condition is the ductwork in?

Flexible foil or plastic duct traps lint more easily than smooth rigid metal. Crushed, disconnected, or poorly sloped sections slow airflow and collect debris. Older buildings may have vent materials or layouts that call for closer attention.

What did the last cleaning find?

Your own service history is the best guide. If a cleaning removes only a light layer of lint, you may be able to keep an annual schedule. If crews find heavy buildup, you may want to shorten the interval. Keep records from each visit so the next decision rests on real information.

paragraphs.header: What is a good starting point for a schedule?
paragraphs.body:
For most apartment buildings, an annual cleaning is a reasonable baseline. Properties with long vent runs, shared risers, heavy usage, or past buildup findings often benefit from cleaning every six months. Very small buildings with short, simple vents may stretch the interval, but only if inspections support it.

These are general guidelines, not promises. A professional inspection of your actual vent system gives you a more reliable answer than any rule of thumb. If you want to know how the work itself goes, our step-by-step guide to dryer vent cleaning explains each stage.

paragraphs.header: What signs mean a vent needs attention sooner?
paragraphs.body:
Your schedule is a plan, but buildings change between visits. Resident reports and maintenance observations can tell you when to move a cleaning up. Common signals include:

  • Laundry taking more than one cycle to dry
  • Dryers or the laundry area feeling unusually hot
  • A lint or burning smell near dryers
  • Lint collecting around the exterior vent opening
  • Exterior vent flaps that don't open fully

Treat these as prompts to schedule an inspection. They are a practical cue to take a closer look, not cause for alarm. Cleaning reduces lint buildup, but it does not remove every risk, so keep dryer filter habits and regular maintenance in place too.

paragraphs.header: How does an occupied building affect scheduling?
paragraphs.body:
Apartment cleanings happen around residents, so planning matters. Good coordination covers notice to tenants, access to units or common areas, and the order of work by floor or building. Our team works with property managers and maintenance teams to keep disruption low.

Many managers ask whether every unit must be entered. The answer depends on how your vent system is built. Your service provider can review your layout and explain which access points are needed.

paragraphs.header: How can you build the schedule into your maintenance calendar?
paragraphs.body:
Put dryer vent cleaning on the same planning calendar as your other recurring work. Many managers set it for a consistent season each year, then adjust after reviewing results. Grouping related services can also cut down on repeat visits to the property. You can see how these fit together on our page for multi-family property services.

A few steps keep the schedule useful:

  1. Record the date, scope, and findings of every cleaning.
  2. Note any resident complaints about drying times or odors.
  3. Review the records each year and adjust the interval.
  4. Reinspect after any ductwork changes or repairs.

Is once a year enough for apartment dryer vents?

For many multi-family buildings, yes. Annual cleaning is a common baseline. Buildings with long vents, shared risers, or heavy use may need cleaning every six months.

Do newer buildings need less frequent cleaning?

Not necessarily. Newer buildings can still collect lint, especially with long or bent vent runs. Inspection results should guide the schedule, not building age alone.

Who is responsible for scheduling dryer vent cleaning?

In most multi-family properties, the owner, management company, or association arranges it. Your lease terms or governing documents may spell out the details for your property.

Does cleaning the vents mean the dryer filter can be skipped?

No. Residents should keep cleaning the lint filter after every load. Professional cleaning handles the ductwork beyond the filter.

Can you adjust the schedule after the first cleaning?

Yes. The first visit shows how much lint your system collects. Many properties tighten or relax the interval based on what the crew finds.
